locator.work: Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (with The English Physician Enlarged), new edn. 1850 — Project Gutenberg eBook #49513, public domain
locator.heading: The Tamarisk Tree

source_text:
IT is so well known in the place where it grows, that it needs no
description.

_Time._] It flowers about the end of May, or June, and the seed is
ripe and blown away in the beginning of September.

_Government and virtues._] A gallant Saturnine herb it is. The root,
leaves, young branches, or bark boiled in wine, and drank, stays the
bleeding of the hæmorrhodical veins, the spitting of blood, the too
abounding of women’s courses, the jaundice, the cholic, and the biting
of all venomous serpents, except the asp; and outwardly applied, is
very powerful against the hardness of the spleen, and the tooth-ache,
pains in the ears, red and watering eyes. The decoction, with some
honey put thereto, is good to stay gangrenes and fretting ulcers, and
to wash those that are subject to nits and lice. Alpinus and Veslingius
affirm, That the Egyptians do with good success use the wood of it to
cure the French disease, as others do with lignum vitæ or guiacum; and
give it also to those who have the leprosy, scabs, ulcers, or the like.
Its ashes doth quickly heal blisters raised by burnings or scaldings.
It helps the dropsy, arising from the hardness of the spleen, and
therefore to drink out of cups made of the wood is good for splenetic
persons. It is also helpful for melancholy, and the black jaundice that
arise thereof.

pubmed.title: In vitro comparative evaluation of Tamarix gallica extracts for antioxidant and antidiabetic activity.
pubmed.relevance_note: Evaluates antidiabetic potential, offering modern context for traditional use regarding 'too abounding of women's courses' and metabolic regulation.

pubmed.title: Multi-targeted therapeutic exploration of Tamarix gallica flowers for anti-ulcer activity and associated complications.
pubmed.relevance_note: Investigates anti-ulcer properties, providing mechanistic insight into traditional applications for 'bleeding of hæmorrhodical veins' and gastrointestinal hemorrhage.

pubmed.title: Chemical profiling of maceration and decoction of Tamarix gallica L. organs and in vitro biological properties.
pubmed.relevance_note: Profiles chemical constituents of decoctions, supporting traditional preparation methods and suggesting mechanisms for treating 'jaundice' via antioxidant activity.

evidence.summary: Modern research supports Tamarix gallica's traditional use in managing hemorrhage (anti-ulcer) and metabolic issues (antidiabetic). Antioxidant properties may address jaundice. Evidence for venomous snake bites is currently absent in retrieved literature.

concordance.rationale: Modern evidence (PMID: 36578220, 39084138) supports antioxidant and anti-ulcer activities but lacks clinical data for historical claims like hemostasis or antivenom.
concordance.uncertainty: High due to absence of specific clinical trials for bleeding, jaundice, or snake bites in current literature.

issues: Unearned Grade C: The entry relies on LLM proposals for taxon resolution without specific historical text evidence to support the 'C' grade; modern pharmacological data (PMID) does not validate historical claims like hemostasis or antivenom, yet the rationale conflates modern findings with historical efficacy without resolving the missing clinical evidence gap.
Incomplete Evidence: The 'HEADING' and 'women's courses' quotes failed verification but no alternative source text was provided to substantiate these specific historical claims within the entry.

Taxon Resolution Uncertainty: Multiple candidates (T. gallica, T. ramosissima, T. chinensis) were proposed with low-to-moderate confidence from LLM sources; the selection of T. gallica lacks explicit textual evidence distinguishing it from the other species in the source material.
